part.title: The history of food preservation

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Helen Ashworth, and today's lecture is about something we rarely stop to think about: how people have kept food from going off. I'm going to look at four methods, drying, salting, canning and refrigeration. And, more importantly, I'll look at how each one changed what people actually ate.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Let's start with drying, which is almost certainly the oldest method. The idea is simple: take the moisture out, and food lasts much longer. Now, people often assume the earliest drying was done over a fire. Actually, that's smoking, which came later. The very first drying relied on the sun and the wind, and in a dry climate that was really all you needed.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Drying had a huge effect on trade. Dried fruit kept for months, so it could be carried enormous distances. Grapes were dried, of course, to make raisins. But in the ancient Mediterranean, the fruit that travelled furthest was the fig. Merchants carried it right across the region, and it turned up in places where nobody could possibly grow it.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Drying also made food much lighter, because most of the weight in fresh food is just water. That made it ideal for people who were always on the move. Hunters used it, certainly. But the group that depended on it most were herders, who followed their animals from one pasture to the next and simply couldn't carry heavy loads.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, let's move on to salting. Salt works by drawing water out of food, and without water, bacteria can't grow. So salted meat or fish could last a whole winter, or a long sea voyage.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: In northern Europe, salting fish was enormously important. You might expect me to say cod, and cod certainly mattered later on. But in the Middle Ages, the fish that fed much of northern Europe was the herring. It was caught in huge numbers in the Baltic and the North Sea and packed into barrels of salt.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Of course, salted food is very salty, and cooks had to deal with that. The usual approach was to soak the meat or fish overnight before cooking it. Most people just used water. But if you look at recipes from wealthier households, they often recommend soaking it in milk, which was thought to give a softer, milder result.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Now, canning is a much more recent invention, and it has a rather interesting origin. At the end of the eighteenth century, the French government wanted a better way to feed its army and navy. So it offered a prize to anyone who could find a reliable way of preserving food. It was eventually won by a confectioner called Nicolas Appert, in 1809, sorry, 1810.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: What surprises many students is that Appert didn't use cans at all. His food was sealed inside glass bottles and then heated in boiling water. Metal cans, made of iron coated in tin, were introduced in Britain a little later, partly because they didn't break so easily.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Early tins were thick and heavy, and the can opener hadn't been invented yet. So how did people get them open? Well, soldiers sometimes used a knife, or even a bayonet. But the instructions printed on some early cans actually told you to use a hammer and a chisel. Not exactly convenient!
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: By the late nineteenth century, though, canned food was cheap, and that really changed diets. Tinned meat and fish became everyday foods for working families. And exotic fruit reached ordinary homes for the first time. Peaches were popular, but the real symbol of this was tinned pineapple, which became a favourite treat in Britain, especially at Sunday tea.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, refrigeration. Before mechanical fridges, the only way to keep things cold was natural ice. Wealthy families stored it in icehouses, often underground. In the nineteenth century, ice was imported into Britain on a large scale. Some of the early shipments came from America, but most of Britain's ice actually came from Norway, where it was cut from frozen lakes in winter.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The real breakthrough, though, was refrigerated shipping. In 1880, sorry, 1882, a ship arrived in London from New Zealand carrying frozen meat that was still perfectly good after more than three months at sea. Frozen beef from Argentina followed later, but that first cargo was mostly mutton, and New Zealand lamb soon became a regular part of the British diet.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And when fridges finally arrived in ordinary kitchens in the twentieth century, people no longer had to shop for fresh food every single day. So, each method didn't just keep food safe. It changed what ended up on the plate. Next week, we'll look at how the supermarket changed things all over again.
turns.speaker: lecturer

questions.prompt: Tinned ______ became a symbol of exotic fruit in British homes
questions.evidence: the real symbol of this was tinned pineapple

explanation.en: Peaches were popular, but the lecturer says tinned pineapple was the real symbol of exotic fruit reaching ordinary homes.
explanation.ru: Персики ("peaches") были популярны, но, по словам лектора, настоящим символом того, что экзотические фрукты дошли до обычных домов, стал консервированный ананас ("tinned pineapple").
